senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the quality of moral purity
senses.comment: In a number of languages the meaning of ἁγνεία and ἁγνότης is expressed idiomatically, for example, to have a clean heart, to not have other thoughts, or to not cover up one’s real desires.

senses.def: pertaining to what is not allowed

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being bad and disgusting on the basis of not being allowed
pertaining to not being covered
pertaining to that which is different in kind or class from all other entities
pertaining to that which is other than some other item implied or identified in a context
(in combination with a past tense, as part of the apodosis of a conditional sentence) pertaining to being certain, in view of particular circumstances of a condition contrary to fact
a marker of the possibility of any number of occurrences of some event
to return to a proper state of mind
glosses: to return to one’s right senses
to come back to one’s senses
senses.comment: ‘To return to one’s senses’ may be rendered as ‘to again think right’ or ‘to no longer think wrong thoughts.’

senses.def: pertaining to something which should not or cannot be used

senses.subdomain: Opposite, Over Against, Across From, Offshore From
senses.def: a position opposite another position, with something intervening

senses.subdomain: Opposite, Over Against, Across From, Offshore From
senses.def: a position over against an object or other position
a marker of opposition or hostility, with the implication that something is done in place of something else

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause a state of moral purity
the metal silver; after gold the next most highly valued metal in the ancient world
senses.comment: As in the case of ‘gold’ (2.49), there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘silver’ in most languages. In 1 Peter 1:18, however, there is a problem in speaking of silver and gold that ‘perish,’ or even as something that can be ‘destroyed,’ since in reality one does not destroy such elements, and silver and gold do not really ‘perish.’ On the other hand, silver and gold can become oxidized and lose their value, especially if they are impure (see 2.60). Therefore, it seems far better to emphasize the lack of value in translating 1 Peter 1:18. A suitable rendering may then be ‘not with things that can lose their value as silver and gold.’

senses.def: silver in the form of stamped coins used as money
(an idiom, literally: silver and gold) a generic expression for currency
the head servant in charge of all those who served at meals or feasts
senses.comment: It is also possible that ἀρχιτρίκλινος in John 2:8 refers to the master of ceremonies or the toastmaster at the feast.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to treat someone in a shameful and dishonorable manner
senses.comment: It is often possible to translate ἀτιμάζω in Mark 12:4 as ‘to make him suffer the way he should not.’

senses.subdomain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
senses.def: to cause someone to have low status involving dishonor and disrespect
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘causing someone to be dishonored’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to cause someone to be laughed at’ or ‘to cause people to wag their heads at someone’ or ‘to cause people to turn away from someone.’

senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
pertaining to one who or that which is or should be detested or regarded as abhorrent
senses.comment: In some languages ‘detestable’ may be rendered as ‘thought to be extremely bad’ or even ‘that which should never even be seen.’

senses.def: (derivative of βοηθέω ‘to help,’ 35.1) one who provides help or assistance
glosses: patron (in the sense of one who supports a person or endeavor)

senses.def: to enter into a marriage relation, applicable either to a man or to a woman
senses.comment: Some interpreters understand γαμίζω in 1 Corinthians 7:38 to mean ‘to give in marriage’ (see 34.72). See also the discussion at 13.32.

senses.def: to cause a person to become married
a recognized expert in Jewish law (including both canonical and traditional laws and regulations)
glosses: one who is learned in the Law
expert in the Law of Moses

senses.def: a person who has acquired a high level of education in a certain body of literature or discipline
senses.comment: In traditional translations γραμματεύς in contexts such as 1 Corinthians 1:20 and Matthew 13:52 has been rendered as ‘scribe,’ but this generally is misleading since the term ‘scribe’ is usually restricted in meaning to one who writes or copies documents. A γραμματεύς in Jewish life of Bible times would have been an expert in the Law or a scholar in the Holy Scriptures and not a mere copier of manuscripts.

senses.def: a city official with responsibility for the records of a town or city and apparently certain responsibilities for maintaining law and order

senses.subdomain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
senses.def: pertaining to that which is pleasing in view of its being acceptable
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to restructure expressions containing ‘acceptable to’ or ‘pleasing to.’ For example, in Acts 10:35 it may be necessary to translate ‘God accepts whoever worships him and does what is right’ or ‘God is pleased with whoever worships him and does what is right.’ Similarly, in 1 Timothy 2:3 one may translate ‘this is good, and God our Savior likes it’ or ‘… is happy because of it.’

senses.def: pertaining to being welcomed or acceptable
senses.comment: In rendering this expression in Luke 4:24 it may be necessary to restructure the relationships somewhat radically, for example, ‘because people of a town do not wish to accept one of their fellow townsmen as a prophet.’

senses.def: pertaining to being appropriate or fitting, with the implication of being favorable
to render assistance or help by performing certain duties, often of a humble or menial nature
senses.comment: In some languages it is essential in communicating the concept of ‘service’ to introduce a specific reference to ‘a servant,’ for example, ‘to help as a servant’ or ‘to assist as one who must,’ and in some contexts it may be useful to employ a phrase such as ‘to help in small things’ or ‘to do the low tasks.’|In rendering ‘your service’ in Revelation 2:19, it may be necessary to say ‘how you help others’ or ‘how you serve others.’

senses.def: (derivative of διακονέω[a] ‘to serve,’ 35.19) the role or position of serving
a procedure for taking care of the needs of people
senses.comment: For another interpretation of διακονία in Acts 6:1, see 57.119.

senses.def: to serve food and drink to those who are eating
(semantic derivative of διακονία[a] ‘to serve,’ 35.19) money given to help someone in need
senses.comment: For another interpretation of διακονέω in Acts 6:1, see 35.38.

senses.def: pertaining to that which is different
the state resulting from not having drunk anything for a period of time
(derivative of δωρέομαι ‘to give, to grant,’ 57.83) that which is given or granted
pertaining to there being no cause or legitimate reason
pertaining to being without any result
senses.comment: In a number of languages an expression such as ‘to be without results’ may be rendered as ‘will accomplish nothing’ or ‘will be as though it had never happened.’

senses.def: pertaining to being without purpose
(derivative of ἐκτίθημι ‘to put out of,’ 85.46) pertaining to being put out and hence exposed (with particular reference to abandoned children)
the process of dying
senses.comment: In a number of languages clear distinctions are made in the use of terms for dying on the basis of the manner or circumstances of death. For example, one term may refer to death primarily as the result of old age, while another term may refer to death caused by sickness, and still other terms may be used for death caused by violence. Careful distinctions must be used in determining the choice of terms based on particular contexts.

senses.def: a man from whose sons Abraham bought a burial place
a position relatively near the speaker, writer, or viewpoint person
senses.comment: Though ὧδε[a] and ἐνθάδε may seem to be rendered in some contexts as ‘to here’ or ‘hither,’ the semantic component of movement is not found in ὧδε[a] or ἐνθάδε, but in other words in the context indicating movement.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to an extremely short period of time between a previous state or event and a subsequent state or event
senses.comment: In a number of contexts there is the implication of unexpectedness; but this seems to be a derivative of the context as a whole and not a part of the meaning of the lexical items.

senses.def: property in which a person was expected to reside, either as the result of ownership or legal contract
senses.comment: In the NT ἔπαυλις occurs only in Acts 1:20 as a quotation of. The immediate reference is to a person’s traditional residence, but the entire passage must be interpreted figuratively as a reference to a person’s expected position or place of service. The phrase γενηθήτω ἡ ἔπαυλις αὐτοῦ ἔρημος may be rendered as ‘may his house become empty’ or ‘may his home be deserted.’

senses.def: to not recall information concerning some particular matter

senses.subdomain: Recalling and Responding with Appropriate Action
senses.def: to not recall and thus to fail to do something
a person in charge of supervising workers
senses.comment: The term ‘foreman’ may be rendered as ‘one who commands the workers’ or ‘one who assigns work to the workers.’

senses.def: a person who guides, directs, and shows concern for
senses.comment: It may be difficult to render appropriately ἐπίτροπος[b] and παιδαγωγός with a combined meaning of guiding and caring for. It may, in fact, be necessary in some instances to use two verbal expressions, for example, ‘to guide and to help’ or ‘to help by leading’ or ‘to care for by leading.’

senses.def: teach that which is different from what should be taught
senses.comment: In rendering ἑτεροδιδασκαλέω in 1 Timothy 1:3, it may be necessary to be specific about the particular doctrine which forms the basis of contrast, for example, ‘that you may order them to stop teaching a doctrine which is different from what has already been taught’ or ‘… from what I have already taught’ or ‘… from what they ought to teach.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to make a good showing, particularly with regard to outward appearances
to suffer the loss of something which one has previously possessed, with the implication that the loss involves considerable hardship or suffering
to be punished, with the implication of suffering damage
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ζημιόομαι in 1 Corinthians 3:15 as meaning simply ‘to suffer loss’ (see 57.69).

senses.def: a generic collective term for all bodies of water (in this sense θάλασσα[a] is contrasted with the sky and the land)
senses.comment: This generic sense of θάλασσα[a] may be expressed in some languages as ‘extensions of water’ or simply as ‘water.’ In other instances it may be necessary to employ a phrase such as ‘lakes and oceans,’ while in certain languages a term for ocean also has a generic sense of any extensive area of water.

senses.def: a particular body of water, normally rather large
senses.comment: The use of θάλασσα[b] to refer to a lake such as the Lake of Galilee (Matthew 4:18; Mark 1:16) or the Lake of Tiberias (John 21:1) reflects Semitic usage, in which all bodies of water from oceans to pools could be referred to by a single term. Normal Greek usage would employ λίμνη lake, pool (1.72).|Many languages make a clear distinction between different types of bodies of water. The three principal bases for differentiation are (1) fresh, brackish, or salty, (2) relative size, that is, large versus small bodies of water, and (3) existence of an outlet. On the basis of this third type of distinction, a term to designate the Sea of Galilee would need to be different from that used in speaking of the Dead Sea, since the Sea of Galilee has an outlet while the Dead Sea does not. Considerable care must be exercised in the choice of terms for such bodies of water, since failure to select the right terms may result in serious distortion of geography and therefore considerable misunderstanding of the geographical setting of biblical events.

senses.def: to crowd in hard against
to cause someone to suffer trouble or hardship
to suffer hardship
pertaining to being sacrificed to a deity
glosses: having been sacrificed to a deity
senses.comment: In some cultures sacrificing is not practiced, and even the idea of killing an animal as a gift to a deity seems not only strange but even abhorrent. In such languages no special term is to be found for sacrifice, and it may therefore be necessary to use a phrase such as ‘to kill an animal and give it to God’ or ‘to kill an animal in honor of God.’ In such cases, however, it is obviously necessary to have some kind of supplementary note or glossary statement which will attempt to explain the significance and function of sacrifice in the Bible.

senses.def: exceptional capability, with the probable implication of personal potential
senses.comment: In a number of languages the expression ‘to love the Lord with one’s strength,’ in the sense of physical strength, is meaningless, and therefore it may be necessary to translate ‘love the Lord your God as completely as you can.’ It is important to note that in a passage such as Mark 12:30 the terms in the series καρδίαψυχήδιάνοια, and ἰσχύς do not refer to completely different parts or aspects of human personality; rather, the four are combined to emphasize the totality of the individual. In some languages the equivalent way of expressing this comprehensive aspect of personality is ‘to love him completely with all you feel and all you think.’

senses.def: the quality of physical strength

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to having been in existence for only a short time
pertaining to that which is new or recent and hence superior to that which is old
pertaining to not being well known previously but being significant

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: pertaining to a point of time preceding another point of time, with a relatively short interval and with the implication of something different
(derivative of καταβαίνω ‘to move down, to descend,’ 15.107) the slope or declivity of an object which one may descend
senses.comment: ἐγγίζοντος δὲ αὐτοῦ ἤδη πρὸς τῇ καταβάσει τοῦ Ὄρους τῶν Ἐλαιῶν ‘he was already approaching the slope of the Mount of Olives’ or ‘he was already approaching the descent of the Mount of Olives’ Luke 19:37. The latter translation could represent the means of descent, namely, ‘the road leading down from the Mount of Olives.’

senses.def: to cease one’s work or activity, resulting in a period of rest
senses.comment: καταπαύω[a] and κατάπαυσις appear to differ in meaning from ἀναπαύομαι[a] and ἀνάπαυσις[b] (23.80) in that the emphasis of καταπαύω[a] and κατάπαυσις is more upon the cessation of activity resulting in rest rather than upon the mere restorative character of rest.

senses.def: a state of mental gloominess and dejection
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be extremely difficult to speak of ‘changing’ one activity into another or one state into another, and so this expression in James 4:9 must often be rendered as ‘instead of laughing, mourn, and instead of being happy, become sad.’

senses.def: the Aramaic equivalent of the Greek name Πέτρος ‘Peter’ (93.296)
the kernel part of fruit, usually grain
senses.comment: A number of languages make distinctions between two quite different types of seed: (1) those produced by grasses (that is to say, grains) and (2) those produced by other types of plants, for example, beans, squash, apples, etc. In all passages employing the Greek terms in this subdomain (κόκκος, σπέρμα[a], σπόρος), it is best to use some expression referring to ‘grain.’

senses.def: (derivative of Κρήτη ‘Crete,’ 93.508) a person who is a native of Crete
pertaining to not being able to speak or talk
pertaining to being unable to hear
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘deaf’ is an idiom, for example, ‘his ears are closed’ or ‘he has no ears’ or ‘his ears are stone.’

senses.def: (derivative of λίθος[a] ‘stone,’ 2.23) pertaining to being made of or consisting of stone
senses.comment: In speaking of objects ‘made of stone’ it may be necessary in some languages to indicate more precisely the manner in which such objects have been formed, for example, ‘hewn out of stone’ or ‘made from stone by chipping.’

senses.def: to practice magic, presumably by invoking supernatural powers
the son of Amos in the genealogy of Jesus
the son of Semein in the genealogy of Jesus
to effect a change of location in space, with the implication that the two locations are significantly different
glosses: to move from one place to another
senses.comment: In view of the specific reference of μετάθεσις in Hebrews 11:5, it is possible to speak of ‘being taken up,’ but the meaning is clearly a significant change of location from one place to another, that is to say, from earth to heaven.

senses.def: a change from one state to another

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to dislike strongly, with the implication of aversion and hostility
senses.comment: Expressions for ‘hatred’ frequently involve idiomatic phrases, for example, ‘to kill in the heart’ or ‘to spit at someone in the heart.’

senses.def: the content of foolish thought
glosses: what is thought to be foolish
senses.comment: In rendering 1 Corinthians 1:18 it is important to recognize that ‘foolishness’ must be defined in terms of the relationship that it has to those who ‘are being destroyed.’ Therefore, it may be important to translate 1 Corinthians 1:18 as ‘those who are being destroyed think that the message concerning the cross is nonsense’ or ‘… makes no sense’ or ‘… simply cannot be understood.’

senses.def: (derivative of Νινευή ‘Nineveh,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who lives in or is a native of Nineveh
to be in severe or great pain
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘the fire’ must be more clearly marked as the causative agent, so that this expression in Luke 16:24 may be restructured as ‘this fire is causing me great pain.’

senses.def: (derivative of ὀδύνη ‘great distress,’ 25.235) to experience great distress or anxiety

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the organ of sight in humans and many animals, occurring in a pair in the face or elsewhere on the head
senses.comment: In a number of languages an important distinction is made between the eyes consisting of the eyeballs and the eyes covered or partially covered by the eyelids. In Matthew 9:29 and Matthew 20:34, Jesus apparently touched the eyelids, not the eyeballs.

senses.def: region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration
glosses: district (though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)
senses.comment: The meanings of γῆ[d], χώρα[b], κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος[c] are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὀφρῦς ‘brow,’ not occurring in the NT) the upper portion of a precipitous or steep contour of a hill or mountain
a dwelling place of the righteous dead in a state of blessedness (generally equated with οὐρανός[b] ‘heaven,’ 1.11)
senses.comment: In some languages ‘paradise’ has been translated by a borrowed term, but more often than not it is rendered by an expression which is roughly equivalent to ‘that wonderful place’ or even ‘that wonderful place in heaven.’|In Revelation 2:7 ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ τοῦ θεοῦ ‘in the paradise of God,’ the reference may reflect somewhat more closely the historical background of this term, which is derived from an Old Persian word meaning ‘enclosure,’ and thus was applied to a ‘garden’ or ‘park.’ For that reason, a number of commentators have believed that in Revelation 2:7, it is appropriate to translate ‘the garden of God,’ especially since in the context the reference is to the fruit of the tree of life.

senses.def: to join surreptitiously with evil intent
glosses: to slip into a group unnoticed

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to take an attempt) to attempt to do something, with the implication of not succeeding
senses.comment: In a number of languages expressions such as πειράζω[d], πειράομαι, and πεῖραν λαμβάνω may be expressed as ‘to start to do something, but not be able to’ or ‘to think that one can do something, but discover it is impossible.’

senses.def: the experience of an event or state which has been acquired
senses.comment: For another interpretation of περιποίησις in 1 Thessalonians 5:9, see 57.62.

senses.def: (derivative of περιποιέομαι ‘to acquire,’ 57.61) that which is acquired, presumably with considerable effort
senses.comment: For another interpretation of περιποίησις in 1 Thessalonians 5:9, see 90.74.

senses.subdomain: Hold a Wrong View, Be Mistaken
senses.def: pertaining to causing someone to be mistaken
to conduct oneself with proper reference to one’s obligations in relationship to others, as part of some community
glosses: to live in relation to others

senses.def: a person who has been given authority to communicate or to act on behalf of a ruler
to have seen something or someone beforehand or prior to an event in question
glosses: to see beforehand to have seen previously
senses.comment: In some languages an adverb such as ‘previously’ must be represented by a clause, for example, ‘before this happened,’ so that one might translate the expression in Acts 21:29 as ‘for they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian even before this happened.’

senses.def: to know about something prior to some temporal reference point, for example, to know about an event before it happens
to strike suddenly and with force
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand προσρήγνυμι in Luke 6:48 as meaning ‘to overflow the stream bed,’ but in view of the occurrence of τῇ οἰκίᾳ ἐκείνῃ, the meaning of ‘strike against’ seems more justified.

senses.def: to change to a state of poverty
senses.comment: In some languages it may be inappropriate to translate literally ‘rich’ and ‘poor,’ since these may have highly specific meanings and inappropriate connotations for the context of 2 Corinthians 8:9. Therefore, it may be necessary to translate ‘although Christ had previously possessed very much, he became one who possessed nothing and he did this for your sake.’

senses.def: a Hebrew king in the genealogy of Jesus

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the flesh of both animals and human beings
senses.comment: Some languages make an important distinction between the flesh of a living person and the flesh of someone who has been killed or who has died. It would be this latter sense which should be reflected in Revelation 19:18. In Romans 2:28 the reference to ‘circumcision in the flesh’ (ἐν σαρκὶ περιτομή) would, however, require the first sense, namely, the flesh of a living person.

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: a living body
senses.comment: Though the reference of σάρξ in 1 Timothy 3:16 is to the physical body, it may be necessary in some instances to translate this as ‘a human being’ or ‘a person,’ that is to say, ‘Christ appeared as a human being’ or ‘Christ became a person.’ Otherwise, the reader might assume that Christ took on the body of someone else or merely indwelt some miraculous human form rather than actually became a human being

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σάρξ[a] ‘flesh,’ 8.63) humans as physical beings
(a figurative extension of meaning of σάρξ[a] ‘flesh,’ 8.63) human nature, with emphasis upon the physical aspects
senses.comment: In a number of languages it would seem strange, if not totally redundant, to speak of ‘physical fathers’ or ‘human fathers’ (Hebrews 12:9), since the term ‘fathers’ would suffice, and any addition would be misleading. In some instances, however, one might use an expression such as ‘our own fathers,’ so as to provide an implied contrast with the heavenly Father. Where it is necessary to qualify the term ‘fathers,’ one may use an expression such as ‘fathers which caused us to be conceived.’

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: a relatively large group of persons regarded as being biologically related
senses.comment: It may be difficult in some languages to clearly distinguish between culture and race as in Mark 7:26. Sometimes this difference can be indicated by saying ‘the woman lived like a Greek, but she was a Syrophoenician’ or ‘… her parents were from Syrophoenicia.’ In translating ‘people of my own race’ in Romans 11:14, it may be necessary to say ‘all my fellow Jews’ or ‘all those people of whom I am a part’ or ‘those people who are my roots’ or ‘… my trunk,’ based on the analogy of a tree trunk and branches.

senses.def: the psychological aspect of human nature which contrasts with the spiritual nature; in other words, that aspect of human nature which is characterized by or reflects typical human reasoning and desires in contrast with those aspects of human thought and behavior which relate to God and the spiritual life
senses.comment: Some scholars understand the meaning of σάρξ[f] as being a person’s lower nature rather than simply human nature, but the distinction between lower nature and higher nature seems to be primarily one arising out of typical Greek thought rather than out of the Semitic background which seems to be so pervasive in the use of the term σάρξ in NT contexts such as 1 Corinthians 1:26. There are, of course, contexts in which σάρξ does refer to that psychological factor in man which serves as a willing instrument of sin and is subject to sin.

senses.def: human nature, particularly in reference to the physical aspect of human life
senses.comment: In some languages one may more appropriately translate this phrase in Galatians 4:23 as ‘was born like any person is’ or ‘was born like people are normally born.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σάρξ[a] ‘flesh,’ 8.63) physical life
(an idiom, literally: desire of the flesh) desire for sexual gratification
(an idiom, literally: flesh and blood) a human being in contrast with a divine being
(an idiom, literally: thorn in the flesh) something which causes serious trouble and difficulty
senses.comment: There are a number of different interpretations of σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί in 2 Corinthians 12:7 (see discussion at 20.27).

senses.def: to cause someone to no longer believe
glosses: to cause to give up believing
to make someone no longer believe
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand σκανδαλίζω in John 6:61 as meaning ‘to cause offense’ (see 25.179).

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σκανδαλίζω ‘to cause to stumble,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause to sin, with the probable implication of providing some special circumstances which contribute to such behavior
to cause someone to experience anger and/or shock because of what has been said or done
glosses: to cause someone to be offended
senses.comment: See discussion at 25.180.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σκανδαλίζομαι ‘to fall into a trap,’ not occurring in the NT) to give up believing what is right and let oneself believe what is false
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand σκανδαλίζομαι in Matthew 13:21 as meaning ‘to let oneself be led into sin’ or ‘to fall into sin as the result of unbelief.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to fall into sin, with the implication of certain contributing circumstances
to be offended because of some action
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to be offended’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to be bitter against’ or ‘to be stung in the heart.’ In some languages, however, the closest equivalent for some contexts is simply ‘to be angered.’

senses.def: to pour out an offering as an act of worship or ritual observance
senses.comment: In some languages it may be almost meaningless to speak of ‘a person being poured out,’ and therefore it may be more appropriate to translate this expression in Philippians 2:17 as ‘but if my blood is to be poured out upon the sacrifice.’ In Philippians 2:17 and in 2 Timothy 4:6 (the other occurrence of σπένδω in the NT), the contexts are highly figurative.

senses.def: act of engaging in war or battle as a soldier
senses.comment: στρατεύω[a] and στρατεία in 1 Timothy 1:18 and 2 Corinthians 10:4 are used figuratively, and it may be essential to mark this figurative usage as a type of simile. For example, in 1 Timothy 1:18 στρατεύομαι may be rendered as ‘you may, so to speak, wage the good battle’ or ‘it is like you are fighting.’ Similarly, in 2 Corinthians 10:4 στρατεία may be rendered as ‘in what is like a battle for us.’

senses.def: to seize and to take along with

senses.comment: In many languages the process of becoming pregnant is expressed in different ways: ‘to begin to become large,’ ‘to receive sperm,’ ‘to let a child enter,’ or ‘to stop bleeding’ (a reference to the cessation of menstrual periods).|The phrases ἐν γαστρί (Luke 1:31) and ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ (Luke 2:21), meaning ‘in the womb,’ may be added to συλλαμβάνω without significant alteration of its meaning.

senses.def: to help by joining in an activity or effort
senses.comment: In a number of instances it is not necessary to specify the joint effort or activity, since this is supplied by the context itself as, for example, in Luke 5:7 in which ‘coming to help’ indicates clearly the joint efforts. But in some languages it may be important to use a specific expression rather than a generic one. Accordingly, ‘to come and help them’ in Luke 5:7 may be rendered as ‘to come and work with them.’

senses.def: to help by joining in an activity or effort
senses.comment: In a number of instances it is not necessary to specify the joint effort or activity, since this is supplied by the context itself as, for example, in Luke 5:7 in which ‘coming to help’ indicates clearly the joint efforts. But in some languages it may be important to use a specific expression rather than a generic one. Accordingly, ‘to come and help them’ in Luke 5:7 may be rendered as ‘to come and work with them.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to act hypocritically along with others
pertaining to weighing a talent or 125 Roman pounds of twelve ounces each or approximately ninety pounds (English weight) or forty kilograms
senses.comment: It may, however, be better to use in Revelation 16:21 an expression with a more general sense, for example, ‘great stones of hail weighing almost a hundred pounds’ or ‘… forty kilos.’

senses.def: any four-footed animal, either wild or domesticated
senses.comment: A high percentage of languages appear to have no generic term to identify all kinds of quadrupeds whether wild or domesticated. Rather, they tend to make quite clear distinctions between wild and domesticated animals, and therefore it may be necessary to indicate both types in those contexts where the reference is to both wild as well as domesticated animals. For example, one may sometimes speak of ‘animals of the grass and animals of the forest’ or ‘animals of the barn and animals of the mountains.’|In Acts 10:12 the reference is primarily to wild animals, since for the most part wild animals would be those designated as unclean. However, swine were also regarded as unclean, and they were domesticated.

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: a period of three months
a song with religious content
to cause to continue to exist subsequent to some temporal reference point
pertaining to what is done in a limited, sparing manner and of negligible quantity or extent
senses.comment: In 2 Corinthians 9:6 φειδομένως is obviously in contrast with the phrase ἐπ᾽ εὐλογίαις ‘abundantly’ (59.56). It may, however, be necessary to indicate clearly the nature of that which is sown or reaped sparingly, for example, ‘the one who plants only a small amount of seed will have only a very small harvest.’

senses.def: a person who murders another person
a container or object made of copper, brass, or bronze
senses.comment: In a number of languages the most natural equivalent of χαλκίον is ‘metal vessel’ or ‘kettle.’

senses.def: to experience pains associated with giving birth
glosses: to suffer pain in connection with giving birth

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of ὠδίν[a] ‘to suffer birth pain,’ 23.54) to suffer intensely (similar to birth pain)
senses.comment: πάντα δὲ ταῦτα ἀρχή ὠδίνων ‘all these things are simply the beginning of great suffering’ Matthew 24:8, a reference to the so-called Messianic woes (see 24.78).
